context: At-Takathur is Makkan, revealed into a culture that kept score. Tribes boasted in numbers, of men, camels, gold, and the commentators relate that clans would even count their dead to win an argument, walking to the graveyard to finish the tally. The surah’s first verse seizes that whole way of being alive in one word, alhakum, it has distracted you, and its second verse follows the distraction to the only place it ever ends: hatta zurtum al-maqabir, until you visit the graves.

The Prophet ﷺ himself gave the surah its sharpest commentary. He recited Alhakum at-takathur and said: the son of Adam says, my wealth, my wealth, and do you own of your wealth anything except what you ate and used up, what you wore and wore out, and what you gave in charity and sent ahead? Everything else, he ﷺ taught, is left for others. The early community heard this surah as an intervention, a hand on the shoulder of a man running a race in the wrong direction.
name_story: The surah is named for at-takathur, rivalry in accumulation, the competition to have more that its first verse indicts. Some early sources cite it as Alhakum, after its opening word, so that even its titles remember the two poles: the pile, and the distraction.

movements.note: The race for more consumes life until the grave visit, and the word visit is its own sermon: the grave too is a stop, not a home, with a journey after it.
Kalla, no indeed, you will come to know, then again, kalla, you will come to know: certainty postponed is announced twice, like two tolls of one bell.
If only you knew with the knowledge of certainty; you will surely see the blaze, then see it with the very eye of certainty, knowledge ripening into sight.
Then, on that Day, you will surely be asked about an-na’im, the delights: cool water, safety, health, every comfort itemized and questioned.

themes.d: Takathur numbs: the pursuit of increase is not condemned here for greed alone but for what it prevents, attention to why we are alive.
Zurtum, you visited: the mildest word in the surah carries its heaviest news, that death is a doorway with something on the other side.
Ilm al-yaqin, knowledge of certainty, becomes ayn al-yaqin, the eye of certainty: what is doubted now will be seen then, and the surah counts down between them.
An-na’im is not a vague word: shade, water, health, safety. The comforts we never counted are counted, and gratitude is the only answer sheet.

heart: At-Takathur read slowly is an interruption, and it is meant to be. Its first word walks into the middle of your scrolling, your comparing, your quiet tallying of what others have, and names the whole activity: alhakum, it has distracted you. The reciter feels the aim of the verse move from seventh-century camels to his own screens without a single word needing translation. Then comes the surah’s masterstroke, the word visit. You will not live in the grave, you will pass through it, and everything you piled stays on this side of the door while everything you sent ahead waits on the other.

The final verse changes the reciter’s relationship with ordinary comfort. You will be asked about the delights: so the cold water becomes a question, the safe street becomes a question, the healthy child becomes a question. The honest reader leaves this surah doing the only sane thing its logic allows, turning delights into gratitude and gratitude into giving, converting the pile into provision for the road.

passages.why: One word, alhakum, names the disease of every acquisitive age including ours.
Stop on the word visit and hear the grave demoted from destination to doorway.
The last verse turns every comfort you own into a question you will answer.

connections.why: Al-Humazah shows the counter at his worst, wealth counted and recounted as if counting could make him last.
Al-Asr is the cure sheet that follows in the mushaf: time is the capital being wasted, and the four rescues spend it rightly.

virtue.text: Reports promising a set reward for reciting At-Takathur are not authentic and should not be relied on. What is sound is the Prophet’s ﷺ own commentary upon reciting it: the son of Adam claims, my wealth, my wealth, yet truly owns only what he ate, wore out, or gave in charity and sent ahead.
virtue.src: the commentary, Muslim 2958; no sound recitation-report
